extracted.intended_audience: general readers, journalists, legal practitioners and advocates interested in comparative defamation law and freedom of expression
extracted.subtask_description: A comparative encyclopedic summary of defamation (libel/slander) laws, defenses, regional trends, and related legal and social practices worldwide, including criminal vs civil regimes and online content issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of criminal defamation (Thailand, Section 326)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever imputes anything to the other person before a third person in a manner likely to impair the reputation of such other person or to expose such other person to be hated or scorned, is said to commit defamation, and shall be punished with imprisonment not exceeding one year or fined not exceeding twenty thousand Baht, or both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory element formulation: (i) imputing something to another person, (ii) published before a third person, (iii) manner likely to impair reputation or expose to hatred/scorn; sanctions include imprisonment and/or fines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation to the family (Thailand, Section 327)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whoever, imputing anything the deceased person before the third person, and that imputation to be likely to impair the reputation of the father, mother, spouse or child of the deceased or to expose that person hated or scorned to be said to commit defamation, and shall be punished as prescribed by Section 326.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extension of criminal defamation to statements about deceased persons that harm reputation of their close relatives; punished under the same penalties as Section 326.

rubrics_metrics.name: Truth as a defence in criminal libel (historical English law / Libel Act 1843)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under English common law, proving the truth of the allegation was originally a valid defence only in civil libel cases; criminal libel was construed as an offence against the public at large. Section 6 of the Libel Act 1843 allowed the proven truth of the allegation to be used as a valid defence in criminal libel cases, but only if the defendant also demonstrated that publication was for the 'public benefit'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defence requires both veracity and showing publication served public benefit — historically limited; highlights difference between civil and criminal approaches to truth as a defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abolition of criminal libel (United Kingdom)
rubrics_metrics.description: The United Kingdom abolished criminal libel on 12 January 2010 by section 73 of the Coroners and Justice Act 2009.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal reform example: criminal libel removed at the national level in the UK; relevant as model for decriminalization trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment and limits on criminal defamation (United States)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fewer than half of U.S. states have criminal defamation laws, but the applicability of those laws is limited by the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution, and the laws are rarely enforced. There are no criminal defamation or insult laws at the federal level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional protections (free speech) constrain criminal defamation; enforcement and scope vary by state; practical effect is limited prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: State-level criminal defamation statutes (U.S.)
rubrics_metrics.description: On the state level, 23 states and two territories have criminal defamation laws on the books (list provided in article); Iowa criminalizes defamation through case law without a statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of jurisdictional variance: whether a jurisdiction has a statute or relies on case law changes prosecutorial and defence strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offshore libel judgments and the SPEECH Act (U.S. protection against foreign libel judgments)
rubrics_metrics.description: American writers and publishers are shielded from the enforcement of offshore libel judgments not compliant under the SPEECH Act (based on New York's 2008 Libel Terrorism Protection Act).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanism limiting enforcement of foreign defamation judgments in the U.S.; relevant in cross-border 'libel tourism' contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof placement
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases — criminal or civil — the burden of proof continued to be on the defendant, and it was rare to have public interest recognized as a defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where the defendant must prove elements (e.g., truth or public interest), risk to speech and journalists increases; shifting burden to plaintiffs is a common critique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trend toward decriminalization
rubrics_metrics.description: There has been an international trend toward decriminalizing defamation: UNESCO and OSCE ran decriminalization campaigns, and a growing number of countries repealed criminal libel or abolished prison terms for defamation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decriminalization reduces risk of imprisonment but may be accompanied by continued civil liability and other restrictions; track regional reforms and court precedents supporting decriminalization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of civil defamation in lieu of criminal prosecutions
rubrics_metrics.description: The use of civil defamation increased, often in lieu of criminal cases, resulting in disproportionate fines and damages, particularly against media and journalists critical of governments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Civil suits can impose high damages and legal costs that chill speech even when criminal penalties are removed; 'strategic lawsuits against public participation' (SLAPPs) are a key concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Libel tourism (forum-shopping for favourable jurisdictions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Libel tourism enabled powerful individuals to limit critical and dissenting voices by shopping around the world for the jurisdictions most likely to approve their defamation suits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiffs may choose plaintiff-friendly forums to obtain favorable judgments or settlements; countermeasures include laws limiting enforcement of foreign judgments (e.g., SPEECH Act).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of defamation laws to online content
rubrics_metrics.description: Countries in every region extended criminal defamation legislation to online content; bloggers appeared before courts and technological advancements strengthened governments' abilities to monitor online content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Online publication is increasingly subject to the same (or enhanced) defamation restrictions; digital intermediaries and platform policies become central to enforcement and takedowns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private intermediaries' liability and preventive censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Private companies could be held responsible for user-generated content made accessible through their servers or services, leading to excessive compliance with takedown notices and preventive censorship ('privatized censorship').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When intermediaries face liability or unclear takedown procedures, they may over-remove content without due process; transparency, judicial oversight, and appeals are relevant safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vaguely worded laws and disproportionate punishments
rubrics_metrics.description: Since 2016, at least 57 laws and regulations across 44 countries were adopted or amended containing vague language or disproportionate punishments, threatening online freedom of expression and press freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vague offences and harsh penalties create legal uncertainty that chills speech; international bodies flag these as threats to free expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of other offences to penalize criticism (terrorism, anti-state, cybercrime, blasphemy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Other legal trends included using charges of terrorism, blasphemy, inciting subversion of state power, acting against the state, and conducting activities to overthrow the state to prosecute journalists and critics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorities may rely on broadly worded public-order or national-security laws rather than explicit defamation statutes to punish speech; defense strategies must consider alternative charges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special protection for public officials and desacato laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Some countries imposed harsher sanctions for defamation involving public officials or heads of state; 'desacato' laws (defamation of public officials) existed and were targeted for repeal by regional bodies like the OAS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher protection for officials reduces the scope for public-interest reporting and criticism; international human-rights bodies often recommend repeal or narrowing of such laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Available defences: truth and public interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Defences to charges of defamation included truth and public interest in at least 21 countries; in some jurisdictions truth/public interest defences are qualified or limited (e.g., fact vs opinion).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The availability and scope of defences materially affect outcomes; narrow definitions (truth limited to factual statements) restrict protection for opinion and commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal obligations on ISPs to monitor content
rubrics_metrics.description: New legal obligations were imposed on Internet service providers to monitor content, as a matter of national security in some regions (e.g., CIS sub-region).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mandated monitoring imposes operational burdens on intermediaries and raises privacy and due-process concerns; such obligations often accompany expanded criminalization of online speech.

rubrics_metrics.name: Influence of regional and international courts and reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Regional courts and international bodies (e.g., African Court, ECtHR, OSCE, UNESCO) influenced reform: the African Court overturned a journalist's conviction in Lohé Issa Konaté, characterizing it as a violation of human-rights treaties; ECHR standards have considered suspended prison sentences for defamation a violation of Article 10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Court precedents and international reports can drive national legal reform and provide defenses in litigation; their persuasive/ binding force varies by jurisdiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defamation of religion and blasphemy laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Debate around defamation of religions and how this impacts the right to free expression continued; many countries retained blasphemy, apostasy or defamation-of-religion laws, and international bodies (UNESCO, UNHRC) have addressed tensions between respect for beliefs and freedom of expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laws protecting religious sentiments are often used to restrict criticism and are a focal point of international human-rights debates; Rabat Plan of Action and similar instruments offer guidance on prohibiting incitement to hatred while protecting expression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Religious and moral legal frameworks regarding harmful speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Religious traditions (Christianity, Islam, Judaism) have moral/legal doctrines addressing harmful speech (detraction, calumny, lashon hara, slander) with corresponding ethical sanctions, remedies, or proposed legal harmonization (e.g., Malaysian proposals to align statutes with Islamic legal principles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Religious frameworks provide normative criteria and sometimes propose distinct remedies or punishments; in some jurisdictions religious principles influence statutory definitions and penalties for defamatory acts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency reporting and platform data on government takedown requests
rubrics_metrics.description: Platform transparency reports (Meta, Google, Twitter) documented a doubling of content-removal requests from governments, law enforcement and executives to approximately 117,000 requests in 2020; Google published rationale data showing 'defamation' and 'privacy and security' as leading justifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Platform data helps track state requests and rationales for takedowns; lack of uniform transparency limits accountability and comparative analysis.
